title: The Critical Role of Itinerant Contributions to Orbital Angular Momentum Relaxation and Dynamics
authors: Andrew C. Grieder, Luis M. Canonico, Frederico Simões, Aron W. Cummings, Yuan Ping
abstract: Orbital angular momentum (OAM) is a promising degree of freedom for low-dissipation transport and magnetization control, yet its relaxation mechanisms remain controversial, with atomcentered approximations (ACA) predicting much shorter OAM diffusion lengths than experiments. We address this discrepancy using first-principles Lindbladian density-matrix dynamics, capturing electron-phonon scattering and itinerant OAM contributions, together with a first-principles parameterized tight-binding approach that separates the ACA and itinerant components. In MoS2,a strong-spin-orbit-coupling (SOC) system, orbital relaxation is multi-timescale, with fast intervalley redistribution followed by slower decay coupled to the spin. In weak-SOC silicene, spin and orbital dynamics decouple; an electric field tunes spin relaxation while leaving orbital lifetimes unchanged. In both materials, ACA orbital lifetimes are at least one order of magnitude shorter than itinerant ones, due to ultrafast precession driven by crystal-field splitting, absent from the itinerant component. These results demonstrate that going beyond atom-centered models is essential for describing orbital relaxation and diffusion.
summary: This work resolves a major theoretical conflict regarding orbital angular momentum (OAM) relaxation in 2D materials by distinguishing between atom-centered (ACA) and itinerant contributions. Using advanced density-matrix simulations, the authors show that the itinerant component, which accounts for momentum-space texture, dictates the true, much longer orbital lifetimes, proving that ACA models are insufficient for accurate predictions.
main_problem: The paper addresses the discrepancy between predicted and experimentally observed orbital angular momentum (OAM) relaxation lengths, noting that atom-centered approximations (ACA) severely underestimate the true relaxation dynamics.
main_result: The itinerant contribution to OAM relaxation, which captures momentum-space texture, is crucial and leads to orbital lifetimes significantly longer (by an order of magnitude) than those predicted by ACA models.
method: The study employs first-principles Lindbladian density-matrix dynamics and a parameterized tight-binding approach to explicitly separate and calculate the contributions of ACA and itinerant OAM components.
model_or_system: The research focuses on 2D materials like $	ext{MoS}_2$ (strong SOC) and silicene (weak SOC), analyzing orbital dynamics under electron-phonon scattering and external electric fields.
key_observables: Orbital lifetimes ($	au_{Lz}$), OAM relaxation dynamics, spin-orbital coupling effects, and the ratio of itinerant to ACA relaxation rates.
important_parameters: Spin-orbit coupling strength (SOC), electric field strength, and the distinction between intravalley and intervalley scattering channels.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the full dynamics must be described by including the itinerant OAM component, moving beyond simplified atom-centered models.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the two distinct timescales of orbital relaxation in $	ext{MoS}_2$, contrast spin/orbital textures for ACA vs. itinerant OAM in silicene, and show the scaling of relaxation rates with momentum scattering rates.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical discrepancy, details the advanced computational methods (FPDMD, TB), applies these methods to $	ext{MoS}_2$ and silicene to characterize the two OAM components, and concludes that the itinerant component governs the long-time dynamics.
why_interesting: The explicit separation and comparison of local (ACA) versus delocalized (itinerant) degrees of freedom in a quantum system is highly relevant to understanding open quantum dynamics and decoherence mechanisms in solid-state devices.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Spin and orbital dynamics of optically excited electrons in MoS2. (a) Spin and orbital relaxation at 300 K. Dashed lines indicate the two decay time scales, 0.25 ps (black) and 6.1 ps (orange, red). (b) Schematics of carrier, spin, and orbital inter- and intra-valley relaxation pathways. (c) Energy-resolved orbital relaxation for only intervalley re- laxation, and (d) intravalley relaxation. The color scale indi- cates normalized orbital polarization.

FIG. 2. Spin and orbital textures and dynamics in silicene near the K valley. (a-c) Band structure at E = 1 V/nm with color indicating (a) spin, (b) atom-centered OAM, and (c) itinerant OAM. Note the opposite (same) sign of Sz (Lz) of the field-split branches. (d-f) Polarization dynamics at E = 0 (dashed) and E = 1 V/nm (solid) for (d) spin by FPDMD at 100 K, (e) atom-centered OAM by TB, and (f) itinerant OAM by FPDMD at 100 K.

FIG. 4. Orbital relaxation rate as a function of momentum relaxation rate, for (a) the TB-ACA and (b) the FPDMD (Berry-phase) OAM at 100 K. Colors denote different applied electric fields. The dashed line in (b) denotes the intrinsic electron-phonon scattering rate.

FIG. 3. Spin and orbital lifetimes in silicene, with the Fermi level at the conduction band minimum, as a function of ap- plied electric field. (a) Lifetimes arising from FPDMD with electron-phonon scattering at 100 K, and (b) lifetimes from real-space TB dynamics with Anderson disorder strength W = 700 meV. In (a), τ EY Sz and τ DP Sz are evaluated from the EY and DP models of spin relaxation. In (b), τ Berry Lz is the or- bital lifetime including the itinerant contributions and τ ACA Lz only considers the atom-centered component.
